# Multivariate Analysis

{{< include shared-code.qmd >}}
{{< include ca-income.qmd >}}

```{r}
pop = pop.earnings 
sam = earnings 
pop$group = pop$sex == 'female'
sam$group = sam$sex == 'female'

xco = function(w,x) {
  w=as.numeric(w)
  x + .15*(2*w-1)
}

sam.dot = list(size=1,    alpha=.15)
pop.dot = list(size=.25,    alpha=.05)
scatter.by.group = function(data, dot=sam.dot, width=sd, 
                            highlight=NULL, 
                            highlight.color='yellow', highlight.alpha=.25,
                            line.alpha = NULL,
                            group.means.alpha=NULL)
                            { 
  p = ggplot(data)
  if(!is.null(highlight)) {
    p = p + annotate('rect', 
                      xmin=min(highlight)-.5,
                      xmax=min(highlight)+.5,
                      ymin=-Inf, ymax=Inf, 
                      fill=highlight.color, alpha=highlight.alpha)
  } 
  if(!is.null(group.means.alpha)) {
    summaries = data |> group_by(group) |> summarize(income=mean(income))
    p = p + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=income, color=group), alpha=group.means.alpha, data=summaries, linetype='dashed') 
  }
  if(!is.null(line.alpha)) { 
    p = p + stat_summary(aes(x=xco(group, education), y=income, color=group), 
    geom='line', alpha=line.alpha, fun=mean, linetype='solid') 
  }

  p + geom_point(aes(x=xco(group, education),  y=income, color=group), 
               size=dot$size, position=position_jitter(seed=0,w=.15), alpha=dot$alpha) +
      stat_summary(aes(x=xco(group, education), y=income, color=group), geom="pointrange", alpha=.7, fun.data=mean_sd)  +
    scale_x() + scale_y() + scale_alpha(range=c(0,1)) + guides(color='none')
}

scatter.by.sex.only = function(data, dot=sam.dot, width=sd) {
    ggplot(data) + 
      geom_point(aes(x=sex,  y=income, color=group), 
                 size=dot$size, position=position_jitter(seed=0,w=.15), alpha=dot$alpha) +
    stat_summary(aes(x=sex, y=income, color=group), geom="pointrange", alpha=.7, fun.data=mean_sd) +
    scale_y() + guides(color='none')
}

money = function(x) { sprintf('%1.0fk', round(x/1000, digits=0)) }  
```

## Multivariate Analysis

```{r}
scatter.by.group(sam)
```

```{r}
muhat.male = mean(sam$income[sam$sex=='male']) 
muhat.female = mean(sam$income[sam$sex=='female'])
```

- Today, we're going to talk about how to analyze data when we have multiple covariates.
- An important application is analyzing disparities to think about discrimination.
- Above, we see the kind of data we'll be working with.
- Each dot represents a California resident, age 25-35, who responded to the CPS.
  - $Y_i$, their income, is on the $y$-axis.
  - $X_i$, their education level, is on the $x$-axis.
  - $W_i$, their sex, is indicated by color. And a slight shift along the $x$-axis.
    - $\ingroupa{W_i=0}$ indicates male, $\ingroupb{W_i=1}$ indicates female.
- As usual, we've drawn in each group's income mean and standard deviation too.
- We'll write $\ingroupa{\hat\mu(0,x)}$ and $\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,x)}$ for the mean income of male and female respondents with $x$ years of education. 

## Plan for Today

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-cap: 
#| - Imaginary Population of California Residents
#| - Real Sample of California Residents from CPS
scatter.by.group(pop, dot=pop.dot)
scatter.by.group(sam)
```

- From a calculational and inferential perspective, this is nothing new.
  - We're still talking about ways of summarizing a sample that's broken down into columns.
  - That our columns are determined by two variables rather than one makes no difference.
- The part that is new will be interpretation and communication.
  - We'll see that there are a variety of ways to look at differences in a multivariate setting.
  - If we're not careful, we can find ourselves talking about different summaries as if they were the same.
- That'll be our focus today.
  - Thinking and communicating precisely about what we're talking about.
  - Understanding how we get different answers to 'the same question' if we're imprecise.
  - Thinking about the implications of what we choose to report.

## Our Data and Approach

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-cap: 
#| - Imaginary Population of California Residents
#| - Real Sample of California Residents from CPS
scatter.by.group(pop, dot=pop.dot)
scatter.by.group(sam)
```

- Our main example will be income disparities that we can see in the CPS. 
- But we'll start by looking at something else: disparities in grad-school admissions.
- We're not going to talk about statistical inference today. 
  - But we're not going to be working with a made-up population either. 
  - Instead, we'll just work with our sample a little recklessly.
- We'll talk as if our summaries of the sample are reasonable descriptions of the population.
  - Even though we know that they're just point estimates.
  - And that point estimates can be pretty far off-target. 

## Where We're Headed {.hidden} 

```{r}
Y = sam$income
X = sam$education
W = sam$sex == 'female'
N1 = sum(W==1)
N0 = sum(W==0)
muhat = Vectorize(function(w,x) { mean(Y[W==w & X==x]) })

muhat.male = mean(Y[W==0])
muhat.female = mean(Y[W==1])
muhat.male.adjusted = mean(muhat(0,X[W==0]))

raw.gap = muhat.female - muhat.male
raw.ratio = muhat.female/muhat.male
adjusted.gap = muhat.female - muhat.male.adjusted
adjusted.ratio = muhat.female / muhat.male.adjusted
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap:
#|  - income vs. sex (aggregated)
#|  - income vs. education and sex (disaggregated)

scatter.by.sex.only(sam)
scatter.by.group(sam, group.means.alpha=.2)
```


:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

Female residents of CA earn \$`r money(-raw.gap)` less, on average, than male ones.
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1)} \ - \  \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0)}  
&\approx \ingroupb{`r money(muhat.female)`} \ - \ \ingroupa{`r money(muhat.male)`} \\
&\approx `r money(raw.gap)` 
\end{aligned}
$$
And `r 100*round(raw.ratio, 2)` cents for every dollar a male one does.
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1)} \ / \ \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0)} 
&\approx \ingroupb{`r money(muhat.female)`} \ / \  \ingroupa{`r money(muhat.male)`} \\
&\approx {`r round(muhat.female/muhat.male, 2)`} \\
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

Female residents earn $`r -adjusted.gap` less than similarly-educated male ones.
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:W_i=1}Y_i} \ - \  \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:W_i=1}}\ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, X_i)}  
&\approx \ingroupb{`r money(muhat.female)`} \ - \ \ingroupa{`r money(muhat.male.adjusted)`} \\
&\approx `r money(adjusted.gap)`
\end{aligned}
$$

And `r 100*round(adjusted.ratio, 2)` cents for every dollar a similarly-educated male one does.
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:W_i=1}Y_i } \ / \ \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:W_i=1}}\ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, X_i)}  
&\approx \ingroupb{`r money(muhat.female)`} \ / \  \ingroupa{`r money(muhat.male.adjusted)`} \\
&\approx {`r round(adjusted.ratio, 2)`} \\
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
::::

::: aside
Don't worry about all the math here. We'll get there. This is just a preview.
:::

# Berkeley Admissions and Simpson's Paradox

## A Famously Paradoxical Example
```{r}
#| fig-asp: .5
Y = c(rep(c(0,1), c(4704, 3738)), 
      rep(c(0,1), c(2827, 1494)))
W = c(rep(0, 4704+3738), rep(1, 2827+1494))

berkeley = data.frame(admit=Y, gender=factor(c('men', 'women'), levels=c('men','women'))[W+1])

dot = pop.dot
ggplot(berkeley) + 
      geom_point(aes(x=gender,  y=admit, color=gender), 
                 size=dot$size, position=position_jitter(seed=0,w=.15,h=.075), alpha=dot$alpha) +
    stat_summary(aes(x=gender, y=admit, color=gender), geom="pointrange", alpha=.7,
                 fun.data=mean_sd) + guides(color='none') + 
                 coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-.1,1.1)) + 
                 scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0,1,by=.2)) + 
                 scale_x_discrete(labels=c('Men', 'Women'))
```

- In the 1970s, Berkeley graduate programs were admitting a much higher proportion of [men]{.groupa} than [women]{.groupb}.
  - $\ingroupa{`r sum(Y[W==0])`/`r sum(W==0)`\approx `r round(100*mean(Y[W==0]))`}$% of men who applied were admitted.
  - $\ingroupb{`r sum(Y[W==1])`/`r sum(W==1)`\approx `r round(100*mean(Y[W==1]))`}$% of women who applied were admitted. 
  - People were concerned that this difference was evidence of discrimination against women.^[We've shifted our focus from  discrimination on the basis of sex to discrimination on the basis of gender. That would've been my preference for the discussion of income disparities too, but the CPS doesn't currently ask about gender identity. You analyze the data you have, not the data you wish you had.]]
$$
\color{gray}
\text{admission rate gap} = \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1} Y_i} - \ingroupa{\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i: W_i=0} Y_i} \approx `r round(mean(Y[W==1]) - mean(Y[W==0]), 2)`
$$

- But, on closer examination, most departments were admitting women at a higher rate than men.
- What's going on?  Let's see if we can figure it out by working with some stylized data.

## 


```{r}
x = c(1,1,1,0,0,0,  1,0,0)
y = c(0,0,0,1,1,1,  1,0,1)
w = c(1,1,0,1,0,0,  1,0,0)
jitter.y = .075*c(0,0,0,0,0,0,    0,0,-1)
jitter.x = -.05*c(-1,0,1,-1,0,1,  0,0,0)  
data = data.frame(x=x, jitter.x=jitter.x, y=y, jitter.y=jitter.y, w=w)
berkeley.data = data

berkeley.scales.nox = list(
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1), labels=c('0', '1/3', '2/3', '1')), 
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-.1,1.1)),
  guides(color='none'))
berkeley.scales = c(list(scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(0,1))), berkeley.scales.nox)

exercise.grid = function(data) { 
  ggplot(data) + geom_point(aes(x=x+jitter.x, y=y+jitter.y), shape=1, size=8) + berkeley.scales
}

solution.grid = function(data, numbered=FALSE) {
  p = exercise.grid(data) 
  if(numbered) { 
    p = p + geom_text(aes(x=x+jitter.x, y=y+jitter.y, label=1:nrow(data)), alpha=.6) 
  }
  p +
    geom_point(aes(x=x+jitter.x, y=y+jitter.y, color=factor(w)), size=8, alpha=.5, 
      data=data) + 
    geom_pointrange(aes(x=x+.01*(2*w-1), y=y, ymin=y-.05, ymax=y+.05, color=factor(w)),  
      data=data |> group_by(w,x) |> summarize(y=mean(y))) +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept=mean.y, color=factor(w)), 
      data=data |> group_by(w) |> summarize(mean.y=mean(y))) 
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r}
ggplot() + geom_blank()
```


```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
```

### What We're Doing

- Above is a stylized version of the Berkeley data in which we have two departments.
  - At the department on the left ($x=0$),  getting in is easy.
  - At the department on the right ($x=1$), getting in is hard.
- We'll draw dots representing applicants. 
  - The $y$-coordinate indicates whether they were admitted ($y=1$) or not ($y=0$).
  - The color of the dot indicates their gender. [Men are red]{.groupa}. [Women are green]{.groupb}.

### Warm-up Exercise
- Color three dots red and three green so that ...
  1. Within each column, the mean of the green dots is *equal to* the mean of the red dots.
  2. The mean of all the green dots is *lower* than the mean of the red ones. 
- Annotate your plot by ...
  1. Drawing in the means of the red and green dot within each column. 
    - Use dots with arms [`r pointrange`]{.groupa} [`r pointrange`]{.groupb} because that's what we usually do in **R**.
    - Don't worry about the length of the arms. We're not thinking about spread here. 
  2. Drawing in the means of *all* the red dots and all the green dots. 
    - Use horizontal lines.  
  
### Paradox Exercise
- Add three more dots --- two red and one green --- so that ...
  1. Within each column, the mean of the green dots is *now higher* the mean of the red ones. 
  2. The mean of all the red dots is *still lower* than the mean of the red ones. 
- Fix your annotations to account for these new dots. 

:::


## The Story our Exercises Tell 
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-cap:
#|  - Warm-up Data
#|  - Paradox Data
solution.grid(data[1:6,])
solution.grid(data)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Warm-up Story
- The story, in this simple example, is that ... 
  - more men apply to the department everybody gets in to. 
  - more women apply to the department nobody gets in to. 
- So men are admitted at a higher rate to the university as a whole.
- Even though men and women are admitted at the same rate within each department.
- **Lesson.** Even when there is no disparity within groups, there can be a disparity in aggregate.

### Paradox Story

- The story in this follow-up, is that ...
  - some woman miraculously get admitted to the department nobody gets in to.
  - some man, equally miraculously, is rejected by the department everybody gets in to.
  - and one more man, less miraculously, gets is admitted to that department too.
- The university as a whole still admits men at a higher rate than women.
- But on a departmental level, that's reversed. Every department admits women at a higher rate than men.
- **Lesson.** Within-group and aggregate disparities can be in *opposite directions*.
  
:::

# Breaking Down Disparities in Admission Rates
Analyzing our caricature of the Berkeley data 

## A Few Summaries of Admission Rates

:::: free-zoom
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7

#y = c(0,0,0,1,1,1,  0,1,1)
#w = c(1,1,0,1,0,0,  0,1,0)
jw = c(-1,1,-1,-1,-1,1, 1,1,0)
berkeley.data$jitter.w = .05*jw
ggplot(berkeley.data) + 
    geom_point(aes(x=w+jitter.w, y=y, color=factor(w)), size=8, alpha=.5) +
    geom_pointrange(aes(x=w, y=y, ymin=y-.05, ymax=y+.05, color=factor(w)), 
      alpha=.7, 
      data=berkeley.data |> group_by(w) |> summarize(y=mean(y))) +
      guides(color='none') + berkeley.scales.nox + scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(0,1), labels=c('Men', 'Women')) +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept=mean.y, color=factor(w)), alpha=.2, 
      data=berkeley.data |> group_by(w) |> summarize(mean.y=mean(y)))
solution.grid(berkeley.data)
```
::::

```{r}
Y = berkeley.data$y 
X = berkeley.data$x
W = berkeley.data$w 
muhat = Vectorize(function(w,x) { mean(Y[W==w & X==x]) })

muhat.male = mean(Y[W==0])
muhat.female = mean(Y[W==1])
```


:::: columns
::: {.column}
### At the Graduate School
The rate for women is `r percent(muhat.male-muhat.female)` lower than for men.
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1)} \ - \  \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0)}  
&\approx \ingroupb{`r round2(muhat.female)`} \ - \ \ingroupa{`r round2(muhat.male)`} \\
&\approx `r round2(muhat.female - muhat.male)` 
\end{aligned}
$$

The rate for women is `r round(muhat.female/muhat.male, 2)` times the rate for men.
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1)} \ / \ \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0)} 
&\approx \ingroupb{`r round2(muhat.female)`} \ / \  \ingroupa{`r round2(muhat.male)`} \\
&\approx {`r round(muhat.female/muhat.male, 2)`} \\
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::: {.column}
### In Department 0
The rate for women is `r percent(muhat(1,0)-muhat(0,0))` higher than for men.
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,0)} \ - \  \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, 0)}  
&\approx \ingroupb{`r round2(muhat(1, 0))`} \ - \ \ingroupa{`r round2(muhat(0, 0))`} \\
&\approx `r round2(muhat(1, 0)-muhat(0, 0))`
\end{aligned}
$$

The rate for women is `r round(muhat(1,0)/muhat(0,0), 2)` times the rate for men. 
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1, 0)} \ / \ \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, 0)} 
&\approx \ingroupb{`r round2(muhat(1, 0))`} \ / \  \ingroupa{`r round2(muhat(0, 0))`} \\
&\approx {`r round2(muhat(1, 0)/muhat(0, 0))`} \\
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::


- Here we see the paradox we talked about before in quantitative terms.
  - When we compare within departments, it looks like women are better-off than men. 
  - But when we look at the university as a whole, this discrepency is reversed.
- These comparisons are relatively simple in that we're just reading two numbers off a plot.
  
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column} 
### On the Left

- We compared means in our plot of the aggregated data.
- This is nice because the result is simple. It's one number.
  
:::
::: {.column}
### On the Right

- We compared columns in the disaggregated data.
- This is nice because it's a 'like-with-like' comparison.

:::
::::

##  What If We Want Simplicity *and* Comparability?

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-cap: 
#|  - The warm-up version 
#|  - The paradox version
solution.grid(berkeley.data[1:6,])
solution.grid(berkeley.data)
```

- **Exercise.** Summarize the typical difference in admission rate ...
  - between [female applicants]{.groupb} and [male applicants]{.groupa} **to the same department**
  - using only one number
- *Step 1*. Do this for both samples above: the 'warm up version' and the 'paradox version'.  
- *Step 2*. Do it in abstract terms using mathematical notation. 
  - Write ${\faded W_i,X_i,Y_i}$ for the values of *gender*, *department*, and *admission status* in our sample.
  - Write $\ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, x)}$ and $\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1, x)}$ for within-group means.
  - Check that when you plug in the numbers for your two samples, you get your answers from Step 1.
- *Step 3*. Do it in terms that make sense when you have more than two departments.
  - That is, generalize your answer to Step 2 so it does what you think it should when $X$ is non-binary.
  - If your answer to Step 2 already worked for non-binary $X$, you have nothing to do here. You're done.
  

## Solution 1. An Average over Departments

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-cap: 
#|  - The warm-up version 
#|  - The paradox version

muhat.frac = Vectorize(function(w,x) { 
  sprintf('\\frac{%d}{%d}', sum(Y[W==w & X==x]), sum(W==w & X==x))
})
solution.grid(berkeley.data[1:6,])
solution.grid(berkeley.data)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Warm-up Version
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{summary} 
&= \frac{1}{D}\sum_{x=1}^D 
\qty{ \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,x)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, x)} } && \qqtext{ for departments } 1 \ldots D \\
&\frac{1}{2}\qty[ \{\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1, 0)} - \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, 0)}\} + \{\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1, 1)} - \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, 1)}\} ] &&\qqtext{ in our examples } \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\qty[ \{ \ingroupb{1} - \ingroupa{1} \} + \{ \ingroupb{0} - \ingroupa{0} \} ] = 0 \\
\end{aligned}
$$

### Paradox Version
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{summary} 
&= \frac{1}{D}\sum_{x=1}^D 
\qty{ \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,x)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, x)} } && \qqtext{ for departments } 1 \ldots D \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\qty[ \{\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1, 0)} - \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, 0)}\} + \{\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1, 1)} - \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, 1)}\} ] &&\qqtext{ in our examples } \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\qty[ \{\ingroupb{`r muhat.frac(1, 0)`} - \ingroupa{`r muhat.frac(0, 0)`}\} \ + \ \{\ingroupb{`r muhat.frac(1, 1)`}-\ingroupa{`r muhat.frac(0, 1)`} \} ] 
&\approx \frac{1}{2}\qty[ \qty{`r round(muhat(1,0) - muhat(0,0), 2)`} + \qty{`r round(muhat(1, 1) - muhat(0, 1), 2)`} ] \\
&\approx `r round(mean(muhat(1,0:1) - muhat(0,0:1)), 2)`
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

- This is telling us the direction of the disparity within departments.
  - In the warm-up version, it's zero because there is no disparity in acceptance rates within departments.
  - In the paradox version, it's positive because [women]{.groupb} are accepted to both more often than [men]{.groupa}.
- But is it a good summary of the experience of the women applying to them? Probably not. 
  - Only 1 applies to Department 0.
  - More---3 in the paradox version---apply to Department 1.
  - And we're giving the same weight to the rate difference in each departments.
- What we get isn't really typical *for women who apply*. 
- We've counted the one who applied to Department 0 ${\faded 3 \times}  more than the ones who applied to Department 1.

## Solution 2. An Average over Applicants
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7

N1 = sum(W==1)
X1 = X[W==1]
stopifnot(N1==4)
solution.grid(berkeley.data[1:6,], numbered=TRUE)
solution.grid(berkeley.data, numbered=TRUE)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Warm-up Version

$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{summary} 
&= \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, X_i) - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0,X_i)} } }  &&\qfor N_w = \sum_{i: W_i=w} 1 \\
&= \ldots 
&= \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}}  0 = 0  &&\qqtext{in the warm-up version} \\
\end{aligned}
$$

### Paradox Version

$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{summary} 
&= \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, X_i) - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0,X_i)} } }  &&\qfor N_w = \sum_{i: W_i=w} 1 \\
&= \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}}  0 = 0  &&\qqtext{in the warm-up version} \\
&= \frac{1}{`r N1`} \qty[\{ \ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, `r X1[1]`)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, `r X1[1]`)} \} + 
\{\ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, `r X1[2]`)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, `r X1[2]`)} \} + 
\{\ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, `r X1[3]`)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, `r X1[3]`)} \} + 
\{\ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, `r X1[4]`)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, `r X1[4]`)} \} ]  &&\qqtext{in the paradox version} \\
&\approx 
\frac{1}{`r N1`} \qty[\{\ingroupb{`r muhat.frac(1, X1[1])`} - \ingroupa{`r muhat.frac(0,X1[1])`}\} +
 \{\ingroupb{`r muhat.frac(1, X1[2])`} - \ingroupa{`r muhat.frac(0,X1[2])`}\} +
 \{\ingroupb{`r muhat.frac(1, X1[3])`} - \ingroupa{`r muhat.frac(0,X1[3])`}\} +
 \{\ingroupb{`r muhat.frac(1, X1[4])`} - \ingroupa{`r muhat.frac(0,X1[4])`}\}] \\
&\approx 
\frac{1}{`r N1`} \qty[\{`r round(muhat(1, X1[1]) - muhat(0, X1[1]), 2)`\} +
\{`r round(muhat(1, X1[2]) - muhat(0, X1[2]), 2)`\} +
\{`r round(muhat(1, X1[3]) - muhat(0, X1[3]), 2)`\} +
\{`r round(muhat(1, X1[4]) - muhat(0, X1[4]), 2)`\}] \\
& \approx `r round(mean(muhat(1,X1) - muhat(0,X1)), 2)`
\end{aligned}
$$

### Paradox Version
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{summary} 
&= \frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1} \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,X_i)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} } 
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

- This is a comparison that focuses on what's typical for women who apply to the Graduate School. 
  - Each female applicant gets equal weight in 'deciding' what is typical. 
  - That's why ${\faded X_i=1}$ occurs in 3 of `r N1` terms. 
- The number we get is not radically different in this case (`r round(mean(muhat(1,X1) - muhat(0,X1)), 2)` vs. `r round(mean(muhat(1,0:1) - muhat(0,0:1)), 2)`), but it can be. 
  - What if many more women had applied to, and been rejected by, Department 1?
  - How would these two summaries compare then?


## Reinterpreting Solution 2

```{r}
scatter.by.group(sam)
```

- We can, in fact, think of this as the average difference between the income of
  - each female respondent's income, $\ingroupb{Y_i}$ 
  - the mean income among males at their level of education, $\ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)}$.

$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{summary} 
&= \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat \mu(1,X_i)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} }  
= \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} \qty{ \ingroupb{Y_i} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} }
\end{aligned}
$$

- These two expressions will always be equal, no matter what the actual values of $W_i,X_i,Y_i$ are.
- We can think of the first one as a version of the second where we sum in a certain order. 

:::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
scatter.by.group(sam)
```

[The same plot as above, for convenience.]{.fg style="color:gray"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i: W_i=w} Y_i 
&\explain{=}{We sum first over dots in a column, then over columns.}
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} Y_i    \\
&\explain{=}{The column sum is the column's mean times its number of dots.}
\sum_{x} \hat \mu(w, x) \times N_{w,x} \qfor N_{w,x} = \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} 1  \\
&\explain{=}{Or equivalently, its mean summed over the dots.}
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \  X_i=x}} \hat \mu(w,x) \\ 
&\mathexplain{=}{\hat\mu(w,x)=\hat\mu(w,X_i) \text{ within a column}.} 
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} \hat \mu(w, X_i) \\
&\explain{=}{We 'unorder' that sum to get back to the form we started with.} 
\sum_{i: W_i=w} \hat \mu(w, X_i)       
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

## Visualizing Averages using Histograms

```{r}
proportion.scale = 300000
scaled.interleaved.bars = list(geom_bar(aes(x=xco(group, education), y=proportion.scale*after_stat(prop), fill=group, color=group), 
                               position='identity', alpha=.03, linewidth=.2), 
                               scale_y(c(0,150000), sec.axis=sec_axis(~./proportion.scale, name='Proportion')),
                               guides(color='none', fill='none'))
bars= list(geom_bar(aes(x=education, y=after_stat(prop), fill=group, color=group), 
                     position='identity', alpha=.05, linewidth=.4), 
            guides(color='none', fill='none'))


scatter.by.group(sam) + scaled.interleaved.bars 
```

- To make sense of our summary, it's helpful to revisit a counting trick we use now and then.
  - When we want to average over the people in a sample, we can use a histogram to help us count.
  - This reduces a sum over hundreds or thousands of people to a sum over a few bins.
- The average of function of $x$ over the education levels of our female respondents  ...
  - is a weighted average of the function's values at each education level ...
  - where an education level's weight is its *frequency*  among female respondents. 
$$
\faded
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} f(X_i) = \sum_{x} f(x) \ingroupb{P_{x\mid 1}} \qfor 
\underset{\faded\text{height of the green bar at $x$}}{\ingroupb{P_{x\mid 1} = \frac{N_{1,x}}{N_1}}}
$$

- Here the function of $x$ we're looking at is $f(x) = \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,x)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0,x)}$.
  - That's the difference in mean income between female respondents and male ones at education level $x$.
  - In visual terms, it's the difference in the height of the [green]{.groupb} and [red]{.groupa} lines. 
- And we're averaging that difference with the weights shown by the [green bars]{.groupb}.

### Proof 

To prove it, we can trace the argument from our last slide backward, stopping in the middle. 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i: W_i=w} f(X_i)  
&\explain{=}{We sum first over dots in a column, then over columns.}
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \  X_i=x}} f(X_i) \\ 
&\mathexplain{=}{f(x)=f(X_i) \text{ within a column}.} 
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} f(x) \\
&\explain{=}{The column sum is the column's mean times its number of dots.}
\sum_{x}f(x) \times N_{w,x} \qfor N_{w,x} = \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} 1  \\
& \qqtext{ so } \\
\frac{1}{N_w} \sum_{i: W_i=w} \hat \mu(w', X_i) 
&= \sum_{x} f(x) \times \frac{N_{w,x}}{N_w} 
\end{aligned}
$$

- If we prefer, we could summarize this disparity by focusing on what's typical for *male respondents*.
  - Or for respondents in general.
  - Or for respondents who, e.g., have not attended college.

### Terminology

- It's common to use the same words to describe each of these summaries.
  - 'The average difference in income between male and female respondents, **adjusted for education**'.
  - Or sometimes '..., *controlling for education*'.^[This can be confusing because it has a different --- but related --- meaning when when we're talking about designing an experiment.]
- This results in a lot of confusion. 
- There is more precise terminology out there. 
  - But it tends to be used when we're talking about differences between groups *receiving different treatments*.
  - We'll get into that more precise terminology next time. 
  - And talk briefly about how it gets used in contexts like this, where we're not talking about treatments.
  - Today, when we talk about the adjusted difference, that'll mean the average over [female respondents]{.groupb}.

### The Raw Difference
Female respondents earn \$`r money(muhat.male-muhat.female)` less, \
on average, than male respondents.
$$
\color{gray}
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:W_i=1} Y_i} \ - \ \ingroupa{\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i:W_i=0} Y_i}  
\approx `r money(muhat.female - muhat.male)` 
$$

### The Adjusted Difference
 \
And they earn `r money(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1])))` less than similarly-educated ones.
$$
\color{gray}
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}}  \qty{ \ingroupb{Y_i} \ - \ \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} }
\approx `r money(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1])))` 
$$

:::
::::

- When people talk about comparisons like this, they're often pretty imprecise with their language.
- Here are a few things you might want to think about when hear about a comparison between two groups.
  1. What's being reported.
    - A raw difference or an adjusted one?
    - What variable(s) are being adjusted for? 
    - What group is being averaged over?
  2. How the things *they could report* might differ.
  3. Why they're reporting what they're reporting.

## The Raw Gap and Covariate Shift 
```{r}
scatter.by.group(sam, group.means.alpha=.2, line.alpha=.2)
```

- When we look at the raw gap in 'histogram form', we can see how it differs from the adjusted one very clearly.
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{raw gap} 
&= \ingreen{\sum_{i:W_i=1} \hat\mu(1,X_i)} - \inred{\sum_{i:W_i=0} \hat\mu(0,X_i)} 
&& \text{sum over people form} \\
&= \sum_{x} \ingreen{P_{x\mid 1} \ \hat\mu(1,x)} - \sum_{x} \inred{P_{x\mid 0} \  \hat\mu(0,x)} 
&& \text{histogram form} \\
&=
\sum_{x} \ingreen{P_{x\mid 1} \ \hat\mu(1,x)} + \sum_{x} (\ingreen{P_{x\mid 1}} - \ingreen{P_{x|1}} - \inred{P_{x\mid 0}}) \ \inred{\hat\mu(0,x)} 
&& \text{adding a fancy version of zero} \\
&= \underset{\text{adjusted gap}}{\sum_{x} \ingreen{P_{x\mid 1}} \ \{\ingreen{\hat\mu(1,x)} - \inred{\hat\mu(0,x)}\} } 
   + \underset{\text{covariate shift term}}{\sum_x \{\ingreen{P_{x\mid 1}} - \inred{P_{x\mid 0}}\} \ \inred{\hat\mu(0,x)}}
&& 
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.panel-tabset}
### The Covariate Shift Term
- It differs by a 'covariate shift term'. 
  - This term that has nothing to do with the income disparity at a given education level.
  - It's about the shift in the distribution of education --- our covariate --- from one group to another.
- In this case, this term is positive. 
  - The raw gap is bigger than the adjusted one. 
  - `r money(muhat.female - muhat.male)`  vs. `r money(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1])))`.
- Let's try to develop some visual intuition about what's going on.

### Visualing Covariate Shift 

- To keep things simple, let's try to forget about the context. 
- Let's think about the covariate shift term ...
- It's the difference of two averages of the same function of x.
  - The function---the red one---
within-column mean male income [`r pointrange`]{.groupa}.
It's the difference of two averages of the same function of x: within-column mean male income [`r pointrange`]{.groupa}.
- This function is increasing with $x$. Income increases with education.
- 
  - The average over the distribution of female education levels: [green bars]{.groupb}
  - The average over the distribution of male education levels: [red bars]{.groupa}
- The
- This is *upward shift* in the distribution of education levels. 
- And the function we're averaging increases from left to right.

### Covariate Shift in Context


 Income increases with education.
- The result is that the *positive*
---is what makes the raw gap bigger than the adjusted one.

an *upward shift* because fe
  - The function we're averaging increases from left to right. Income increases with education.
  - The distribution we're averaging over *shifts* from left to right. 
    - From the distribution of education among [male residents. Red bars.]{.groupa}.
    - To the distribution of education among [female respondents (green bars)]{.groupb}.
  - And 
  - So the [green bars]{.groupb} tend to be higher than the [red bars]{.groupa} on the left side of the plot.

:::


## Another Visualization of Covariate Shift

```{r}
facet.by.group = list(facet_grid(row=vars(group)), theme(strip.background=element_blank(), strip.text=element_blank()))
ggplot(sam) + bars + facet.by.group
``` 

- These are exactly the same histograms we had overlaid on the previous plot. They're exactly the same bars.
- What's changed is *layout*. Our groups are shown one above the other rather than interleaved as before.
- This makes it easier to see that the [red one]{.groupa} has more mass *on the left* side than the [green one]{.groupb}.


## Covariate Shift *reduces* this Disparity
::: free-zoom
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
scatter.by.group(sam) + scaled.interleaved.bars
ggplot(sam) + bars + facet.by.group
```
:::

- Our plot shows that, at virtually all levels of education, male respondents out-earn female ones.
- And the typical magnitude of this disparity is something like \$15k.
  - Sometimes it's about \$20k (e.g. at 11, 14, and 18 years of education)
  - Sometimes it's about \$10k (e.g. at 16 years)
- That's summarized reasonably by the adjusted difference, \$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1]))))`.
  The raw difference, \$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1]) - mean(Y[W==0])))`, is much smaller. 
- So we're seeing that covariate shift *reduces* the disparity --- it makes it smaller than what we see within levels.
- That's two factors working together.
  1. *A Downward Shift*. Male respondents tend to have less education than female ones.
  2. *An Upward Trend*.   Income tends be higher at higher levels of education.
- The relationship between the raw and adjusted difference depends on both. 


## Solution 1. An Average over Levels of Education

```{r}
scatter.by.group(sam)
```

```{r}
years = sort(unique(sam$education))
years.str = paste(years, collapse=', ') 
```

$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{summary} 
&= \frac{1}{`r length(years)`}\sum_{x \in \text{years}}  
\qty{ \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,x)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, x)} } \qfor \text{years} =\{ `r years.str ` \}  \quad (`r length(years)` \text{ levels}) \\
&= \frac{\{\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1, 8)} - \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, 8)}\} + \{\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1, 9)} - \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, 9)}\} + \ \ldots \ + \{\ingroupb{\hat\mu(1, 20)} - \ingroupa{\hat\mu(0, 20)}\}}{`r length(years)`} \\
&\approx \frac{  \{ \ingroupb{`r money(muhat(1, 8))`}-\ingroupa{`r money(muhat(0, 8))`}\} \ + \ \{\ingroupb{`r money(muhat(1, 9))`}-\ingroupa{`r money(muhat(0, 9))`} \} + \ \ldots \ + \{ \ingroupb{`r money(muhat(1, 20))`}-\ingroupa{`r money(muhat(0, 20))`} \} }{`r length(years)`} \\
&\approx \frac{  \{`r money(muhat(1, 8) - muhat(0, 8))`\} + \{`r money(muhat(1, 9) - muhat(0, 9))`\} \ + \ldots \ + \{`r money(muhat(1, 20) - muhat(0, 20))`\}}{`r length(years)`} \\
&\approx `r money(mean(muhat(1, years) - muhat(0, years)))` 
\end{aligned}
$$

- This is, coincidentally, the same as the difference for respondents with 12 years of education.^[After rounding to the nearest \$100.]
- But is it a good summary of how much less female respondents are making? Probably not. 
  - Very few---only `r sum(X[W==1]==8)`---have 8 years of education.
  - Many---`r sum(X[W==1]==12)`---have 12 years of education.
  - And we're giving the same weight to the mean difference at each level of education.
- What we get isn't necessarily typical *for female respondents*.
- We've counted the ones with 8 years of education 
$`r sum(X[W==1]==12)`/`r sum(X[W==1]==8)` \approx `r round(sum(X[W==1]==12)/sum(X[W==1]==8))`$ times more than the ones with 12. 

## Solution 2. An Average over Respondents
```{r}
scatter.by.group(sam)
```

$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{summary} 
&= \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, X_i) - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0,X_i)} } }  \qfor N_w = \sum_{i: W_i=w} 1 \\
&= \frac{ \{ \ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, `r X[W==1][1]`)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, `r X[W==1][1]`)} \} + 
\{\ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, `r X[W==1][2]`)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, `r X[W==1][2]`)} \} + 
\ \ldots \ +
\{\ingroupb{\hat \mu(1, `r X[W==1][N1]`)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, `r X[W==1][N1]`)} \} }{`r N1`} \\
&\approx \frac{ \{\ingroupb{`r money(muhat(0, X[W==1][1]))`} - \ingroupa{`r money(muhat(1, X[W==1][1]))`}\} +
\{ \ingroupb{`r money(muhat(1, X[W==1][2]))`} - \ingroupa{`r money(muhat(0, X[W==1][2]))`} \} +
\ \ldots \ +
\{ \ingroupb{`r money(muhat(1, X[W==1][N1]))`} - \ingroupa{`r money(muhat(0, X[W==1][N1]))`}\}  }{`r N1`} \\
&\approx \frac{ \{`r money(muhat(1, X[W==1][1]) - muhat(0, X[W==1][1]))`\} +
\{`r money(muhat(1, X[W==1][2]) - muhat(0, X[W==1][2]))`\} +
\ \ldots \ +
\{`r money(muhat(1, X[W==1][N1]) - muhat(0, X[W==1][N1]))`\} }{`r N1`} \\
& \approx `r money(mean(muhat(1,X[W==1]) - muhat(0,X[W==1])))`
\end{aligned}
$$

- This is a comparison that focuses on what's typical *for our female respondents*.
- Each female respondent gets equal weight in 'deciding' what is typical. 
  - That's why $X_i=13$ occurs twice in the three (of `r N1`) terms we actually write out above.
  - It's a fairly common level of education.
    
## Reinterpreting Solution 2

```{r}
scatter.by.group(sam)
```

- We can, in fact, think of this as the average difference between the income of
  - each female respondent's income, $\ingroupb{Y_i}$ 
  - the mean income among males at their level of education, $\ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)}$.

$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{summary} 
&= \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat \mu(1,X_i)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} }  
= \ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} \qty{ \ingroupb{Y_i} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} }
\end{aligned}
$$

- These two expressions will always be equal, no matter what the actual values of $W_i,X_i,Y_i$ are.
- We can think of the first one as a version of the second where we sum in a certain order. 

:::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
scatter.by.group(sam)
```

[The same plot as above, for convenience.]{.fg style="color:gray"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i: W_i=w} Y_i 
&\explain{=}{We sum first over dots in a column, then over columns.}
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} Y_i    \\
&\explain{=}{The column sum is the column's mean times its number of dots.}
\sum_{x} \hat \mu(w, x) \times N_{w,x} \qfor N_{w,x} = \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} 1  \\
&\explain{=}{Or equivalently, its mean summed over the dots.}
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \  X_i=x}} \hat \mu(w,x) \\ 
&\mathexplain{=}{\hat\mu(w,x)=\hat\mu(w,X_i) \text{ within a column}.} 
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} \hat \mu(w, X_i) \\
&\explain{=}{We 'unorder' that sum to get back to the form we started with.} 
\sum_{i: W_i=w} \hat \mu(w, X_i)       
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

## Visualizing Averages using Histograms

```{r}
proportion.scale = 300000
scaled.interleaved.bars = list(geom_bar(aes(x=xco(group, education), y=proportion.scale*after_stat(prop), fill=group, color=group), 
                               position='identity', alpha=.03, linewidth=.2), 
                               scale_y(c(0,150000), sec.axis=sec_axis(~./proportion.scale, name='Proportion')),
                               guides(color='none', fill='none'))
bars= list(geom_bar(aes(x=education, y=after_stat(prop), fill=group, color=group), 
                     position='identity', alpha=.05, linewidth=.4), 
            guides(color='none', fill='none'))


scatter.by.group(sam) + scaled.interleaved.bars 
```

- To make sense of our summary, it's helpful to revisit a counting trick we use now and then.
  - When we want to average over the people in a sample, we can use a histogram to help us count.
  - This reduces a sum over hundreds or thousands of people to a sum over a few bins.
- The average of function of $x$ over the education levels of our female respondents  ...
  - is a weighted average of the function's values at each education level ...
  - where an education level's weight is its *frequency*  among female respondents. 
$$
\faded
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} f(X_i) = \sum_{x} f(x) \ingroupb{P_{x\mid 1}} \qfor 
\underset{\faded\text{height of the green bar at $x$}}{\ingroupb{P_{x\mid 1} = \frac{N_{1,x}}{N_1}}}
$$

- Here the function of $x$ we're looking at is $f(x) = \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,x)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0,x)}$.
  - That's the difference in mean income between female respondents and male ones at education level $x$.
  - In visual terms, it's the difference in the height of the [green]{.groupb} and [red]{.groupa} lines. 
- And we're averaging that difference with the weights shown by the [green bars]{.groupb}.

### Proof 

To prove it, we can trace the argument from our last slide backward, stopping in the middle. 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i: W_i=w} f(X_i)  
&\explain{=}{We sum first over dots in a column, then over columns.}
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \  X_i=x}} f(X_i) \\ 
&\mathexplain{=}{f(x)=f(X_i) \text{ within a column}.} 
\sum_{x} \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} f(x) \\
&\explain{=}{The column sum is the column's mean times its number of dots.}
\sum_{x}f(x) \times N_{w,x} \qfor N_{w,x} = \sum_{\substack{i: W_i=w, \ X_i=x}} 1  \\
& \qqtext{ so } \\
\frac{1}{N_w} \sum_{i: W_i=w} \hat \mu(w', X_i) 
&= \sum_{x} f(x) \times \frac{N_{w,x}}{N_w} 
\end{aligned}
$$


## Variations

- If we prefer, we could summarize this disparity by focusing on what's typical for *male respondents*.
  - Or for respondents in general.
  - Or for respondents who, e.g., have not attended college.

    1. As you'd describe the people in them, e.g. 'all female respondents'.
    2. As you'd describe the dots in the plot, e.g. 'all green dots'

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
scatter.by.group(sam) + scaled.interleaved.bars 
```

:::
::: column
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_1 
&\explain{=}{All male respondents. All red dots} 
\ingroupa{\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i: W_i=0}} \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,X_i)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} } \\
\Delta_2 
&\explain{=}{All female respondents. All green dots} 
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}} \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,X_i)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} } \\
\Delta_3 
&\explain{=}{All respondents who didn't attend college. All dots in the leftmost 4 (pairs of) columns.} 
\frac{1}{N_{x \le 12}}\sum_{i: X_i \le 12} \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,X_i)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} } \qfor N_{x \le 12} = \sum_{i: X_i \le 12} 1  \\
\Delta_4 
&\explain{=}{All respondents outright. All dots.} 
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{ \ingroupb{\hat\mu(1,X_i)} - \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} } 
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

### Terminology

- It's common to use the same words to describe each of these summaries.
  - 'The average difference in income between male and female respondents, **adjusted for education**'.
  - Or sometimes '..., *controlling for education*'.^[This can be confusing because it has a different --- but related --- meaning when when we're talking about designing an experiment.]
- This results in a lot of confusion. 
- There is more precise terminology out there. 
  - But it tends to be used when we're talking about differences between groups *receiving different treatments*.
  - We'll get into that more precise terminology next time. 
  - And talk briefly about how it gets used in contexts like this, where we're not talking about treatments.
  - Today, when we talk about the adjusted difference, that'll mean the average over [female respondents]{.groupb}.

# Covariate Shift

The thing behind the paradox.

## Comparisons with and without Adjustment

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap:
#|  - income vs. sex (aggregated)
#|  - income vs. education and sex (disaggregated)

scatter.by.sex.only(sam)
scatter.by.group(sam, group.means.alpha=.2)
```

:::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### The Raw Difference
Female respondents earn \$`r money(muhat.male-muhat.female)` less, \
on average, than male respondents.
$$
\color{gray}
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:W_i=1} Y_i} \ - \ \ingroupa{\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i:W_i=0} Y_i}  
\approx `r money(muhat.female - muhat.male)` 
$$

:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
### The Adjusted Difference
 \
And they earn `r money(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1])))` less than similarly-educated ones.
$$
\color{gray}
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}}  \qty{ \ingroupb{Y_i} \ - \ \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} }
\approx `r money(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1])))` 
$$

:::
::::

- When people talk about comparisons like this, they're often pretty imprecise with their language.
- Here are a few things you might want to think about when hear about a comparison between two groups.
  1. What's being reported.
    - A raw difference or an adjusted one?
    - What variable(s) are being adjusted for? 
    - What group is being averaged over?
  2. How the things *they could report* might differ.
  3. Why they're reporting what they're reporting.

::: aside
The averages shown in the plot on the left ---  the average incomes of all [male]{.groupa} and [female]{.groupb}
respondents --- are included as faint dashed horizontal lines in the plot on the right.
:::


## What's the Difference?

```{r}
scatter.by.group(sam, group.means.alpha=.2)
```

:::: columns

::: {.column width="52%"}
### The Raw Difference

$$
\color{gray}
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i:W_i=1} Y_i} \ - \ \ingroupa{\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i:W_i=0} Y_i}  
\approx `r money(muhat.female - muhat.male)` 
$$

is what we get when we ...
  
::: {.incremental}
  1. Look at the height of each [red dot]{.groupa}.
  2. Subtract the average height of *all of the [green dots]{.groupb}*.
  3. Average these differences.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### The Adjusted Difference
$$
\color{gray}
\ingroupb{\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i: W_i=1}}  \qty{ \ingroupb{Y_i} \ - \ \ingroupa{\hat \mu(0, X_i)} }
\approx `r money(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1])))` 
$$

is what we get when we ...

  1. Look at the height of each [red dot]{.groupa}.
  2. Subtract the average height of the \
  [green dots]{.groupb} in the same column.
  3. Average these differences.
:::
::::

## The Raw Gap and Covariate Shift 
```{r}
scatter.by.group(sam, group.means.alpha=.2, line.alpha=.2)
```

- When we look at the raw gap in 'histogram form', we can see how it differs from the adjusted one very clearly.
$$
\color{gray}
\begin{aligned}
\text{raw gap} 
&= \ingreen{\sum_{i:W_i=1} \hat\mu(1,X_i)} - \inred{\sum_{i:W_i=0} \hat\mu(0,X_i)} 
&& \text{sum over people form} \\
&= \sum_{x} \ingreen{P_{x\mid 1} \ \hat\mu(1,x)} - \sum_{x} \inred{P_{x\mid 0} \  \hat\mu(0,x)} 
&& \text{histogram form} \\
&=
\sum_{x} \ingreen{P_{x\mid 1} \ \hat\mu(1,x)} + \sum_{x} (\ingreen{P_{x\mid 1}} - \ingreen{P_{x|1}} - \inred{P_{x\mid 0}}) \ \inred{\hat\mu(0,x)} 
&& \text{adding a fancy version of zero} \\
&= \underset{\text{adjusted gap}}{\sum_{x} \ingreen{P_{x\mid 1}} \ \{\ingreen{\hat\mu(1,x)} - \inred{\hat\mu(0,x)}\} } 
   + \underset{\text{covariate shift term}}{\sum_x \{\ingreen{P_{x\mid 1}} - \inred{P_{x\mid 0}}\} \ \inred{\hat\mu(0,x)}}
&& 
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.panel-tabset}
### The Covariate Shift Term
- It differs by a 'covariate shift term'. 
  - This term that has nothing to do with the income disparity at a given education level.
  - It's about the shift in the distribution of education --- our covariate --- from one group to another.
- In this case, this term is positive. 
  - The raw gap is bigger than the adjusted one. 
  - `r money(muhat.female - muhat.male)`  vs. `r money(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1])))`.
- Let's try to develop some visual intuition about what's going on.

### Visualing Covariate Shift 

- To keep things simple, let's try to forget about the context. 
- Let's think about the covariate shift term ...
- It's the difference of two averages of the same function of x.
  - The function---the red one---
within-column mean male income [`r pointrange`]{.groupa}.
It's the difference of two averages of the same function of x: within-column mean male income [`r pointrange`]{.groupa}.
- This function is increasing with $x$. Income increases with education.
- 
  - The average over the distribution of female education levels: [green bars]{.groupb}
  - The average over the distribution of male education levels: [red bars]{.groupa}
- The
- This is *upward shift* in the distribution of education levels. 
- And the function we're averaging increases from left to right.

### Covariate Shift in Context


 Income increases with education.
- The result is that the *positive*
---is what makes the raw gap bigger than the adjusted one.

an *upward shift* because fe
  - The function we're averaging increases from left to right. Income increases with education.
  - The distribution we're averaging over *shifts* from left to right. 
    - From the distribution of education among [male residents. Red bars.]{.groupa}.
    - To the distribution of education among [female respondents (green bars)]{.groupb}.
  - And 
  - So the [green bars]{.groupb} tend to be higher than the [red bars]{.groupa} on the left side of the plot.

:::


## Another Visualization of Covariate Shift

```{r}
facet.by.group = list(facet_grid(row=vars(group)), theme(strip.background=element_blank(), strip.text=element_blank()))
ggplot(sam) + bars + facet.by.group
``` 

- These are exactly the same histograms we had overlaid on the previous plot. They're exactly the same bars.
- What's changed is *layout*. Our groups are shown one above the other rather than interleaved as before.
- This makes it easier to see that the [red one]{.groupa} has more mass *on the left* side than the [green one]{.groupb}.


## Covariate Shift *reduces* this Disparity
::: free-zoom
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
scatter.by.group(sam) + scaled.interleaved.bars
ggplot(sam) + bars + facet.by.group
```
:::

- Our plot shows that, at virtually all levels of education, male respondents out-earn female ones.
- And the typical magnitude of this disparity is something like \$15k.
  - Sometimes it's about \$20k (e.g. at 11, 14, and 18 years of education)
  - Sometimes it's about \$10k (e.g. at 16 years)
- That's summarized reasonably by the adjusted difference, \$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1]))))`.
  The raw difference, \$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1]) - mean(Y[W==0])))`, is much smaller. 
- So we're seeing that covariate shift *reduces* the disparity --- it makes it smaller than what we see within levels.
- That's two factors working together.
  1. *A Downward Shift*. Male respondents tend to have less education than female ones.
  2. *An Upward Trend*.   Income tends be higher at higher levels of education.
- The relationship between the raw and adjusted difference depends on both. 

# More Income Examples 

## Covariate Shift *increases* this other Disparity
```{r}
adj.mf.ca = mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1]))
raw.mf.ca = mean(Y[W==1]) - mean(Y[W==0])
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
georgia.state.code = 13
ga.sam = income(georgia.state.code)$sample
```

```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
this.sam = ga.sam |> 
  mutate(group = race == 'Black only') |> 
  filter(race %in% c('Black only', 'White only'))

W = this.sam$group
X = this.sam$education
Y = this.sam$income
N1 = sum(W==1)
N0 = sum(W==0)
muhat = Vectorize(function(w,x) { mean(Y[W==w & X==x]) })
```

::: free-zoom
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
scatter.by.group(this.sam) + scaled.interleaved.bars
ggplot(this.sam) + bars + facet.by.group
```
:::


- Here we're making the same comparison, but for [Black]{.groupb} and [white]{.groupa} respondents in Georgia.
- The within-group differences are similar (using the same dot colors) to the ones we've just looked at.
  - The trend is still upward --- more education means more income.
  - And [Black]{.groupb} respondents make less at most levels of education, esp. the common ones.
- But the covariate shift is in the opposite direction.
  - [Black]{.groupb} respondents tend to have fewer years of education than [white ones]{.groupa}. 
- As a result, the raw difference is *larger* than the adjusted one. Covariate shift *increases* the disparity.
  - The adjusted difference is about \$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1]))))`. The raw one is about \$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1]) - mean(Y[W==0])))`.
- This is a bigger shift --- and in the opposite direction --- compared to what we saw in the previous example.
  - That was \$`r money(abs(adj.mf.ca))` adjusted &rarr; \$`r money(abs(raw.mf.ca))` raw.  

## Sometimes there isn't much Covariate Shift

```{r}
this.sam = sam 
this.sam$group = (\() runif(nrow(this.sam)) <= .5) |> with_seed(10)

W = this.sam$group
X = this.sam$education
Y = this.sam$income
N1 = sum(W==1)
N0 = sum(W==0)
muhat = Vectorize(function(w,x) { mean(Y[W==w & X==x]) })
```

::: free-zoom
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
scatter.by.group(this.sam) + scaled.interleaved.bars
ggplot(this.sam) + bars + facet.by.group
```
:::

- We're back in California comparing respondents in two *randomly assigned* groups.
  - I flipped a coin for each to decide whether they're [red]{.groupa} or [green]{.groupb}.
- Because of randomization, there isn't really any covariate shift.
  - The distribution of education is the same in both groups. The bars are the same height.
  - As a result, the raw disparity (\$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1]))))`) is 
  about the same as the adjusted one (\$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1]) - mean(Y[W==0])))`).
- There's also little difference in mean income --- at any level --- between the groups. That's why both are about \$0.
- But if we did something as a result of the coin flip, e.g. gave one group a treatment, that might *induce* a difference.
- Next class, we'll see how randomization can help us estimate this induced difference---the treatment's effect.


## Sometimes Covariate Shift is Complicated
```{r}
this.sam = sam |> 
  filter(race %in% c('Black only', 'White only')) |> 
  mutate(group = race == 'Black only') 

W = this.sam$group
X = this.sam$education
Y = this.sam$income
N1 = sum(W==1)
N0 = sum(W==0)
muhat = Vectorize(function(w,x) { mean(Y[W==w & X==x]) })
```

::: free-zoom
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
scatter.by.group(this.sam) + scaled.interleaved.bars
ggplot(this.sam) + bars + facet.by.group
```
:::

- Now we're comparing [Black]{.groupb} and [white]{.groupa} respondents in California.
- Here we see a more complicated pattern of covariate shift---a shift toward the center.
  - [Black]{.groupb} respondents tend to have *less extreme* levels of education than [white ones]{.groupa}.
  - Visually, the [green bars]{.groupb} are higher in the middle than the [red ones]{.groupa}.
- In a sense, the  rightward shift on the left side compensates for a leftward shift on the left side.
- As a result, we don't see a big difference in the raw and adjusted differences.
  - The adjusted difference is about \$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1] - muhat(0,X[W==1]), na.rm=TRUE)))` 
  - The raw difference is about \$`r money(abs(mean(Y[W==1]) - mean(Y[W==0])))`.

### Exercise

*Context*. You're writing an article about income disparities in the US. 

1. Flip a coin. \

  - **Tails**. It's on the disparity between [female]{.groupb} and [male]{.groupa} residents of California.  
  - **Heads**. It's on the disparity between [Black]{.groupb} and [white]{.groupa} residents of Georgia.
    
2. You're going to include one summary in your headline---either the raw or the adjusted difference. Decide which.

3. Write down, in a sentence or two, why you chose what you did.
